hld-building-blocks:0.prompt: You need to route /api/* to one backend pool and /static/* to another, based on the HTTP path. Which kind of load balancer can do this?
options: An L4 load balancer, because it sees the TCP port
An L7 load balancer, because it parses the HTTP request
Either one, since both see the destination IP
Only a DNS-based load balancer using SRV records
hld-building-blocks:0.explanation: Path-based routing requires reading the HTTP request line, which only an L7 (application-layer) balancer does. An L4 balancer works on IP/port tuples and never inspects the HTTP payload, so the port alone can't distinguish /api from /static.

hld-building-blocks:0.prompt: Requests to your service vary wildly in cost: some take 5 ms, some take 2 s. Round-robin is leaving some backends overloaded while others idle. Which algorithm is the best fit?
options: Weighted round-robin with static weights
IP hash so each client sticks to one backend
Least outstanding requests (least connections)
Random selection with no weighting
hld-building-blocks:0.explanation: Least-connections/least-outstanding-requests adapts to actual in-flight work, so slow requests naturally steer new traffic elsewhere. Static weighted round-robin only helps when backends differ in capacity, not when request costs vary unpredictably.

hld-building-blocks:0.prompt: Your health check hits GET /health, which also queries the shared database. During a brief DB slowdown, the LB marks every backend unhealthy and the site goes fully down. What is the best fix?
options: Raise the health check interval from 5 s to 60 s
Remove health checks and rely on client retries instead
Make /health check the DB with a longer timeout only
Keep the liveness check local and handle dependency failures in-app
hld-building-blocks:0.explanation: A health check that depends on a shared dependency turns a partial outage into a total one: every node fails at once and the LB has nowhere to send traffic. Keep the LB check about the instance itself and degrade gracefully on DB errors. A longer interval only delays the same cascade.

hld-building-blocks:0.prompt: An L4 load balancer is placed in front of servers that hold long-lived WebSocket connections. After adding two new servers, they receive almost no traffic for hours. Why?
options: L4 balancers cannot forward WebSocket traffic at all
Existing connections stay pinned; only new connections get rebalanced
The new servers failed health checks because of TLS
Round-robin skips servers that were added after startup
hld-building-blocks:0.explanation: Balancing happens per connection. Long-lived connections stay on their original server until they close, so new capacity only fills as clients reconnect. Fixes include connection draining or periodic reconnects. L4 balancers forward WebSockets fine since they're just TCP.

hld-building-blocks:0.prompt: What is the main reason teams pick an L4 load balancer over an L7 one for a high-throughput service?
options: Lower latency and overhead since it doesn't parse or terminate HTTP
It supports cookie-based sticky sessions natively
It can retry failed HTTP requests on another backend
It can rewrite headers and add request IDs
hld-building-blocks:0.explanation: L4 balancers forward packets/connections without parsing application data, so they are cheaper and faster per request. Cookie stickiness, HTTP retries and header rewriting all need HTTP awareness, which is L7.

hld-building-blocks:0.prompt: You use IP-hash load balancing for session stickiness. Most of your traffic comes from a few large corporate NATs. What problem will you most likely see?
options: Sessions will be lost on every request
Health checks will stop working for hashed backends
TLS handshakes will fail because the IP changes
A few backends get a disproportionate share of the load
hld-building-blocks:0.explanation: Many users behind one NAT share a source IP, so IP hashing sends all of them to the same backend, creating hot spots. Sessions are kept, not lost, which is exactly what makes the load skew stick.

hld-building-blocks:0.prompt: A backend is removed from the pool during a deploy, and in-flight requests to it fail with 502s. Which LB feature prevents this?
options: Active health checks with a shorter interval
Connection draining (deregistration delay)
Switching from least-connections to round-robin
Enabling HTTP keep-alive between LB and backend
hld-building-blocks:0.explanation: Connection draining stops sending new requests to the instance but lets in-flight ones finish before it's removed. Faster health checks only detect failure sooner; they don't protect requests already in progress.

hld-building-blocks:0.prompt: Which capabilities generally require an L7 (HTTP-aware) load balancer rather than L4? Select all that apply.
options: Routing by Host header to different services
Distributing TCP connections across backends
Cookie-based session affinity
Retrying an idempotent GET on another backend after a 503
Preserving the client's source IP via direct server return
hld-building-blocks:0.explanation: Host routing, cookie affinity and HTTP-level retries all need the balancer to parse HTTP. Spreading TCP connections is the core L4 job, and direct server return is an L4 technique where responses bypass the balancer.

hld-building-blocks:0.prompt: A backend is flapping: it passes and fails health checks every few seconds. Which settings help avoid sending traffic to it while it's unstable? Select all that apply.
options: Require several consecutive successes before marking it healthy
Use passive health checks (outlier detection) based on real errors
Lower the unhealthy threshold to a single successful check
Remove the health check timeout entirely
Eject outliers for a cool-down period that grows on repeat failures
hld-building-blocks:0.explanation: Healthy/unhealthy thresholds add hysteresis, outlier detection reacts to real failing traffic, and growing ejection periods stop fast flip-flopping. Re-admitting after one success makes flapping worse, and no timeout means a hung backend is never detected.

hld-building-blocks:0.prompt: An L7 load balancer that terminates TLS can inspect HTTP headers and route on them, but the connection from the LB to the backend is a separate connection.
options: True
False
hld-building-blocks:0.explanation: True. Terminating TLS lets the L7 balancer read the HTTP request, and it then opens (or reuses) its own connection to the backend, optionally re-encrypting. That's why the backend sees the LB's IP and needs X-Forwarded-For for the client IP.

hld-building-blocks:0.prompt: Power of two random choices (pick two random backends, send to the less loaded one) performs much worse than plain random selection when the balancer's load information is slightly stale.
options: True
False
hld-building-blocks:0.explanation: False. Power of two choices is popular precisely because it gets most of the benefit of least-loaded selection while being robust to stale data. Always picking the single least-loaded backend with stale info is what causes herding, where everyone piles onto the same node.

hld-building-blocks:1.prompt: Which responsibility best distinguishes an API gateway from a plain reverse proxy?
options: Forwarding client requests to backend servers
Hiding backend server IPs from the internet
Enforcing API concerns like auth, rate limits and API keys per route
Terminating TLS connections from clients
hld-building-blocks:1.explanation: A reverse proxy forwards requests, hides backends and often terminates TLS. An API gateway adds API-level cross-cutting policy such as authentication, per-client rate limiting, quotas and request transformation. Forwarding and TLS termination are common to both.

hld-building-blocks:1.prompt: Behind Nginx, your Node.js (Express) app logs every request as coming from 10.0.0.5, so per-user rate limiting doesn't work. What is the correct fix?
options: Read req.socket.remoteAddress instead of req.ip
Have Nginx set X-Forwarded-For and configure Express 'trust proxy' for it
Trust whatever X-Forwarded-For value the client sends
Rate limit on the User-Agent header instead
hld-building-blocks:1.explanation: The proxy is the TCP peer, so the socket address is always the proxy. Nginx should append the client IP to X-Forwarded-For and Express should trust only that proxy hop. Trusting arbitrary client-supplied X-Forwarded-For lets attackers spoof IPs and dodge rate limits.

hld-building-blocks:1.prompt: A mobile app needs data from 5 microservices to render one screen, causing 5 round trips over a slow network. Which gateway pattern addresses this?
options: Circuit breaker on each microservice call
Sticky sessions at the gateway
Response caching with a 1-hour TTL
Request aggregation / Backend-for-Frontend at the gateway
hld-building-blocks:1.explanation: A BFF or aggregating gateway makes the 5 calls over the fast internal network and returns one combined response, cutting mobile round trips. Circuit breakers improve resilience, not round-trip count, and long TTL caching would serve stale personalised data.

hld-building-blocks:1.prompt: Every request passes through a single API gateway cluster. What is the most important risk to plan for?
options: It becomes a shared failure point and bottleneck for all traffic
It forces all services to use the same programming language
It prevents services from being deployed independently
It makes TLS impossible between internal services
hld-building-blocks:1.explanation: A gateway on the critical path is a shared dependency: misconfiguration, overload or a bad deploy takes down everything. Run it redundantly, keep business logic out of it and deploy it carefully. It does not constrain service languages or independent deploys.

hld-building-blocks:1.prompt: A team starts putting order-validation rules and pricing logic into the API gateway's plugins to 'avoid duplicating code'. What is the main problem?
options: Gateways cannot run custom code at all
It makes TLS termination slower
Business logic in the gateway couples teams and makes it a deploy bottleneck
Gateways strip request bodies before plugins run
hld-building-blocks:1.explanation: Gateways should hold cross-cutting concerns (auth, rate limits, routing). Domain logic there couples every team to one shared component, so changes need gateway deploys and failures spread widely. Most gateways can run custom plugins, which is why this anti-pattern happens.

hld-building-blocks:1.prompt: Which of these is a forward proxy rather than a reverse proxy?
options: Nginx in front of three app servers
A CDN edge serving your site's assets
An API gateway validating JWTs
A corporate proxy that employees' browsers use to reach the internet
hld-building-blocks:1.explanation: A forward proxy acts for clients reaching arbitrary servers; a reverse proxy acts for servers, receiving client traffic for them. Nginx in front of app servers, CDN edges and API gateways all sit in front of servers, so they're reverse proxies.

hld-building-blocks:1.prompt: Your gateway retries any failed upstream call up to 3 times. During a backend slowdown, traffic to the backend jumps about 4x and it falls over completely. What is the best mitigation?
options: Increase the retry count so more requests eventually succeed
Use a retry budget with backoff and jitter, and retry only idempotent calls
Disable timeouts so requests never fail and need retries
Move retries from the gateway into every client instead
hld-building-blocks:1.explanation: Unbounded retries amplify load exactly when the backend is struggling (a retry storm). A retry budget caps extra traffic, backoff with jitter spreads it out, and limiting retries to idempotent calls avoids duplicate side effects. Moving retries to clients still multiplies load.

hld-building-blocks:1.prompt: Which concerns are reasonable to centralise in an API gateway? Select all that apply.
options: Validating JWTs and rejecting unauthenticated calls
Per-API-key rate limiting and quotas
Calculating discounts for a shopping cart
Request/response logging and correlation IDs
Deciding whether an order can be refunded
hld-building-blocks:1.explanation: Auth checks, rate limits and logging/tracing are cross-cutting and apply to many services, which is what gateways are for. Discount calculation and refund eligibility are domain rules that belong in the owning service.

hld-building-blocks:1.prompt: Nginx is a reverse proxy in front of a Node.js app. Which benefits does this setup commonly provide? Select all that apply.
options: Buffering slow clients so Node isn't tied up by slow uploads
Serving static files without hitting Node
Automatically making the Node app's database queries faster
TLS termination and HTTP/2 handling at the edge
Guaranteeing exactly-once processing of POST requests
hld-building-blocks:1.explanation: Reverse proxies buffer slow clients, serve static assets efficiently and terminate TLS/HTTP/2. They have no effect on DB query speed, and they can't guarantee exactly-once POST handling; that needs idempotency keys in the app.

hld-building-blocks:1.prompt: Using a service mesh sidecar (like Envoy) for service-to-service traffic removes any need for an API gateway at the edge.
options: True
False
hld-building-blocks:1.explanation: False. A mesh handles east-west (internal) traffic: mTLS, retries, internal routing. The edge gateway handles north-south traffic from external clients: public auth, API keys, quotas, public routing. Many systems run both.

hld-building-blocks:1.prompt: If the gateway authenticates a JWT and forwards the request, backend services that are reachable directly on the internal network should still not blindly trust identity headers like X-User-Id from any caller.
options: True
False
hld-building-blocks:1.explanation: True. If anything else on the network can reach the service, a forged X-User-Id header bypasses the gateway's check. Use network policy, mTLS or a signed internal token so services can verify the caller really is the gateway.

hld-building-blocks:2.prompt: What is the key difference between a pull CDN and a push CDN?
options: Pull CDNs fetch from origin on a cache miss; push CDNs get content uploaded ahead of time
Pull CDNs only serve video; push CDNs only serve images
Push CDNs fetch from origin on each request; pull CDNs never contact origin
Pull CDNs require you to manage TTLs; push CDNs ignore Cache-Control
hld-building-blocks:2.explanation: A pull CDN lazily fetches from origin when an edge misses, then caches it. A push CDN has you upload content to the CDN in advance. Neither is limited by media type, and both respect expiry settings in some form.

hld-building-blocks:2.prompt: Your CDN hit ratio for product images is only 20%. URLs look like /img/123.jpg?utm_source=email&session=abc. What is the most likely cause?
options: The images are too large for the edge cache
The CDN is configured as push instead of pull
The origin is sending Content-Type: image/jpeg
Tracking and session query params are part of the cache key
hld-building-blocks:2.explanation: If the full query string is in the cache key, each unique utm/session value creates a separate cache entry, so almost every request misses. Strip irrelevant params from the cache key. Content-Type headers don't affect hit ratio.

hld-building-blocks:2.prompt: You deploy a new app.js and want users to get it immediately while still caching assets for a year. What's the standard approach?
options: Set Cache-Control: no-cache on app.js
Purge the whole CDN on every deploy
Use content-hashed filenames (app.3f9a1c.js) with long max-age and immutable
Set a 60-second TTL on all JavaScript files
hld-building-blocks:2.explanation: Fingerprinted filenames make each version a new URL, so it can be cached forever while the HTML points to the new name right away. Full purges are slow and cause an origin load spike; short TTLs give up most of the caching benefit.

hld-building-blocks:2.prompt: After a full CDN purge, your origin's CPU spikes to 100% and latency climbs. What's happening and what helps most?
options: The CDN switched to push mode; switch back to pull
Every edge misses at once; use origin shield and request collapsing
Purges disable gzip; re-enable compression at origin
The purge invalidated TLS certificates at the edges
hld-building-blocks:2.explanation: A purge empties every edge, so hundreds of POPs miss together and hammer origin. An origin shield (a middle cache tier) and request collapsing (one origin fetch per object, others wait) shrink that fan-in. Purges don't affect compression or certificates.

hld-building-blocks:2.prompt: An API returns different JSON for logged-in users, and you put a CDN in front of it. Some users report seeing another user's account data. What's the most likely misconfiguration?
options: The CDN cached personalised responses under a key without the user identity
The CDN's TTL was set too short
The origin returned Cache-Control: private
The CDN used HTTP/2 to talk to origin
hld-building-blocks:2.explanation: If personalised responses are cached under a URL-only key, the first user's response is served to everyone. Mark them Cache-Control: private/no-store, or bypass the cache for authenticated requests. Cache-Control: private would have prevented this, not caused it.

hld-building-blocks:2.prompt: Which header lets an origin give the CDN a different TTL than browsers, for example 1 day at the edge but 60 s in the browser?
options: Expires
ETag
Cache-Control: s-maxage
Last-Modified
hld-building-blocks:2.explanation: s-maxage applies only to shared caches (CDNs and proxies) and overrides max-age for them, so browsers keep the shorter max-age. Expires is an absolute date for all caches; ETag and Last-Modified are for revalidation, not TTL.

hld-building-blocks:2.prompt: A news site wants pages cached at the edge, but when an article is corrected, the fix must appear within seconds. Which design fits best?
options: No caching for article pages at all
Rely on a 24-hour TTL and ask readers to hard refresh
Push all articles to the CDN once a day
Long edge TTL plus tag/surrogate-key purge triggered by the CMS on edit
hld-building-blocks:2.explanation: Tag-based (surrogate key) purges let the CMS invalidate exactly the affected pages within seconds while keeping long TTLs for everything else. Disabling caching gives up the CDN benefit, and a daily push or long TTL can't meet a seconds-level requirement.

hld-building-blocks:2.prompt: Which practices improve CDN cache hit ratio? Select all that apply.
options: Normalising or removing irrelevant query parameters from the cache key
Adding Vary: User-Agent to all responses
Using an origin shield tier between edges and origin
Serving stale content while revalidating in the background
Setting a unique Set-Cookie on every static asset response
hld-building-blocks:2.explanation: Cleaner cache keys, a shield tier and stale-while-revalidate all increase hits. Vary: User-Agent splits the cache across thousands of UA strings, and many CDNs won't cache responses that set cookies.

hld-building-blocks:2.prompt: Which kinds of content are good candidates for a push CDN rather than a pull CDN? Select all that apply.
options: A large game patch released at a known time to millions of users
Per-user dashboard JSON
A small site whose assets rarely change and are known in advance
Search results generated per query
A video library prepared before a launch event
hld-building-blocks:2.explanation: Push suits content known ahead of time, especially big files with a predictable surge, so edges are warm before demand arrives. Per-user and per-query responses are dynamic and unbounded, so they can't be pre-uploaded.

hld-building-blocks:2.prompt: Using a CDN reduces latency for users mainly because the edge server is geographically closer, cutting round-trip time for TCP/TLS handshakes and data transfer.
options: True
False
hld-building-blocks:2.explanation: True. Edges terminate connections near the user, so the handshakes and data transfer cover a short distance, and cache hits never travel to origin at all. Even misses benefit, since the edge often keeps warm connections to origin.

hld-building-blocks:2.prompt: A CDN purge request takes effect at all edge locations worldwide instantly and atomically, so no user can get the old version after the purge API returns.
options: True
False
hld-building-blocks:2.explanation: False. Purges propagate to many POPs and take from milliseconds to minutes depending on the provider, and browsers may still hold their own copies. That's why versioned URLs are preferred for things that must change atomically.

hld-building-blocks:3.prompt: In the cache-aside pattern, who is responsible for loading data into the cache on a miss?
options: The cache itself fetches from the DB automatically
The database pushes changes into the cache
The application reads the DB and writes the result to the cache
A background job preloads every key at startup
hld-building-blocks:3.explanation: In cache-aside (lazy loading) the application checks the cache, and on a miss reads the DB and populates the cache. When the cache loads from the DB itself, that's read-through.

hld-building-blocks:3.prompt: With cache-aside, a service updates a user row in the DB and then updates the cache with the new value. Two concurrent updates sometimes leave the cache permanently stale. What's the usual fix?
options: Update the cache first, then the DB
Increase the cache TTL
Write to the cache twice to be safe
Delete (invalidate) the cache key after the DB write instead of setting it
hld-building-blocks:3.explanation: With two writers, their DB writes and cache sets can interleave so the cache ends up with the older value forever. Deleting the key after the DB write makes the next read reload fresh data. A short TTL as a safety net also helps; a longer TTL makes it worse.

hld-building-blocks:3.prompt: What is the main risk of write-back (write-behind) caching?
options: Data acknowledged to the client can be lost if the cache fails before flushing
Every write is slower because it waits for the database
Reads always miss because writes skip the cache
It cannot be used with key-value stores
hld-building-blocks:3.explanation: Write-back acknowledges the write once it's in the cache and flushes to the DB later, so a cache crash can lose acknowledged writes. Slower writes is the trade-off of write-through, the opposite pattern.

hld-building-blocks:3.prompt: A product catalog is read thousands of times per second and edited a few times a day. Edits must show up within about a second. Which approach fits best?
options: Write-back caching with hourly flushes
No cache; scale the DB with read replicas only
Cache-aside with invalidation on edit plus a TTL as a safety net
Write-around with a 24-hour TTL
hld-building-blocks:3.explanation: Read-heavy, rarely changed data is the classic cache-aside case. Invalidating on edit gives near-immediate freshness and the TTL limits damage from a missed invalidation. Write-around with a 24 h TTL would serve stale data for up to a day.

hld-building-blocks:3.prompt: Which statement correctly describes write-through caching?
options: Writes go only to the DB; the cache is filled on the next read
Writes go to the cache and the DB synchronously before acknowledging
Writes go to the cache and are flushed to the DB asynchronously
Writes go to the cache only; the DB is a read-only replica
hld-building-blocks:3.explanation: Write-through updates cache and store in the same write path, so the cache stays consistent at the cost of write latency. Writing only to the DB is write-around; asynchronous flushing is write-back.

hld-building-blocks:3.prompt: You use cache-aside. The DB write succeeds but the following cache DELETE fails because of a network blip. What's the consequence and a reasonable mitigation?
options: Nothing; the cache detects DB changes on its own
The DB write is rolled back automatically
Reads fail with errors until the cache restarts
The stale value persists until TTL; retry the delete or invalidate via change data capture
hld-building-blocks:3.explanation: Cache and DB aren't updated atomically, so a failed delete leaves stale data until the TTL expires. Mitigations: retry invalidation (e.g. via an outbox), drive invalidation from the DB's change stream/CDC, and always set a TTL. Caches don't watch the DB by themselves.

hld-building-blocks:3.prompt: A system logs millions of view-count increments per minute and can tolerate losing a few seconds of counts on a crash. Which strategy is most suitable?
options: Write-back: increment in Redis and flush aggregates to the DB periodically
Write-through: update Redis and the DB on every increment
Cache-aside: invalidate the counter key on every increment
No cache: run UPDATE ... SET views = views + 1 for each view
hld-building-blocks:3.explanation: High-frequency writes where small loss is acceptable suit write-back: batching turns millions of DB writes into a few. Write-through or per-view UPDATEs would hammer the DB, and invalidating on every increment defeats the cache.

hld-building-blocks:3.prompt: Which statements about read-through vs cache-aside are correct? Select all that apply.
options: In read-through, the cache layer loads missing data from the store
Cache-aside keeps the application in control of what gets cached
Read-through means writes are never needed to keep data fresh
Both can serve stale data unless writes invalidate or update the cache
Cache-aside requires the cache to understand the database schema
hld-building-blocks:3.explanation: Read-through puts the loading logic in the cache layer; cache-aside keeps it in the app. Both need a write-side strategy (invalidate, update or TTL) or they go stale. Read-through doesn't remove that need, and in cache-aside the cache knows nothing about the schema.

hld-building-blocks:3.prompt: You use write-through caching for user profiles. Which issues should you still plan for? Select all that apply.
options: Higher write latency because both writes happen in the request path
Caching data that is written but never read (cache pollution)
Partial failure where the DB write succeeds but the cache write fails
Reads of profiles that were cached never hitting the cache
Automatic cross-region consistency with no extra work
hld-building-blocks:3.explanation: Write-through adds write latency, caches everything written (even never-read data), and still faces partial failures between two systems. Reads of cached data do hit the cache, and it gives no cross-region consistency by itself.

hld-building-blocks:3.prompt: Write-around caching (write only to the DB, populate the cache on read) helps avoid filling the cache with data that is written once and rarely read.
options: True
False
hld-building-blocks:3.explanation: True. Write-around skips the cache on writes, so only data that is actually read gets cached. The trade-off is that the first read after a write is always a miss.

hld-building-blocks:3.prompt: If you delete the cache key before writing to the DB (instead of after), cache-aside can no longer serve stale data under concurrent reads.
options: True
False
hld-building-blocks:3.explanation: False. A concurrent reader can miss right after the delete, read the old DB value and re-cache it before the write commits, leaving stale data. That's why people delete after the write, sometimes with a delayed second delete.

hld-building-blocks:4.prompt: A popular cache key with a 5-minute TTL expires, and within a second 2,000 requests miss and all query the DB, which slows to a crawl. What is this called?
options: Cache penetration
Cache stampede (thundering herd)
Cache pollution
Write amplification
hld-building-blocks:4.explanation: A stampede is many concurrent misses on the same key all rebuilding it at once. Cache penetration is repeated lookups for keys that don't exist at all, which also bypass the cache but for a different reason.

hld-building-blocks:4.prompt: Which technique most directly prevents a stampede on a single expensive key?
options: Increase the cache's memory size
Switch the eviction policy from LRU to LFU
Lower the TTL so the key is refreshed more often
Let only one request rebuild the key (lock or single-flight) while others wait or get stale data
hld-building-blocks:4.explanation: Request coalescing (a mutex, SET NX lock or in-process single-flight) means one caller recomputes and the rest wait or get the stale value. More memory or a different eviction policy doesn't stop many simultaneous misses on an expired key.

hld-building-blocks:4.prompt: Your cache holds a small set of items accessed constantly, plus a nightly batch job that scans millions of keys once. After each batch run the hit rate collapses. Which eviction policy is most resistant to this?
options: LFU, because frequently used items outrank one-time scans
LRU, because recently scanned items are evicted first
FIFO, because it ignores access patterns
TTL-only expiry with no size limit
hld-building-blocks:4.explanation: A one-off scan touches each key once. Under LRU those keys look 'recent' and push out the real hot set. LFU ranks by frequency, so the hot items survive. FIFO also evicts the hot set, and no size limit just runs out of memory.

hld-building-blocks:4.prompt: You cache 10,000 keys at deploy time, all with TTL = 3600 s. Exactly an hour later, the DB gets a burst of load. What's the simplest fix?
options: Use LRU instead of TTL
Add jitter to TTLs (e.g. 3600 s ± 10%)
Shorten the TTL to 60 s
Store all keys in a single hash
hld-building-blocks:4.explanation: Keys written together with the same TTL expire together (synchronized expiry). Random jitter spreads expiries out. A shorter TTL just causes the burst more often, and LRU is a capacity policy, not a freshness one.

hld-building-blocks:4.prompt: One Redis key (a celebrity's profile) gets 200k reads/s and saturates one Redis Cluster node while others are idle. What's the most effective fix?
options: Add more nodes to the cluster
Change the key's TTL to 1 second
Replicate the hot key: cache it in-process or as N suffixed copies spread across nodes
Switch the maxmemory-policy to allkeys-lfu
hld-building-blocks:4.explanation: A single key lives on one slot, so adding nodes doesn't split its traffic. Local in-process caching or N copies (key#1..key#N, read a random one) spreads load. A shorter TTL or a different eviction policy doesn't change where the key lives.

hld-building-blocks:4.prompt: Attackers request random product IDs that don't exist. Each lookup misses the cache and hits the DB. What's a standard defence?
options: Use a longer TTL on existing products
Switch from LRU to LFU eviction
Shard the database by product ID
Cache negative results briefly and/or use a Bloom filter of valid IDs
hld-building-blocks:4.explanation: This is cache penetration. Caching 'not found' with a short TTL, or checking a Bloom filter of existing IDs before the DB, stops the misses reaching the DB. TTLs and eviction policies only affect keys that exist.

hld-building-blocks:4.prompt: Probabilistic early expiration (e.g. the XFetch algorithm) helps prevent stampedes by:
options: Having requests randomly recompute a value shortly before its TTL ends, with rising probability
Doubling the TTL every time a key is accessed
Evicting keys with the lowest access count first
Refusing all reads while a key is being recomputed
hld-building-blocks:4.explanation: Each reader near expiry has a small, increasing chance of refreshing early, so one request usually rebuilds the value before it expires and no herd forms. It doesn't change TTLs or eviction order, and it doesn't block reads.

hld-building-blocks:4.prompt: Which strategies help with a stampede on a hot key that is expensive to compute? Select all that apply.
options: Serve the stale value while one worker refreshes it in the background
Use a distributed lock (e.g. Redis SET key val NX PX) so one worker recomputes
Give all keys the same TTL so they're easy to reason about
Refresh the key proactively before it expires
Disable the cache for that key during peak hours
hld-building-blocks:4.explanation: Stale-while-revalidate, a recompute lock and proactive refresh all stop many callers recomputing at once. Identical TTLs cause synchronized expiry, and turning off the cache sends every request to the backend.

hld-building-blocks:4.prompt: In Redis 7, which maxmemory-policy values may evict keys that have no TTL set? Select all that apply.
options: allkeys-lru
volatile-lru
allkeys-lfu
volatile-ttl
allkeys-random
hld-building-blocks:4.explanation: allkeys-* policies consider every key. volatile-* policies only evict keys with an expiry set, so if no keys have TTLs they behave like noeviction and writes fail with OOM errors once memory is full.

hld-building-blocks:4.prompt: LRU evicts the item that hasn't been accessed for the longest time, regardless of how many times it was accessed before that.
options: True
False
hld-building-blocks:4.explanation: True. LRU only looks at recency. An item accessed 10,000 times an hour ago is evicted before one accessed once a second ago. LFU is the policy that weighs access frequency.

hld-building-blocks:4.prompt: Redis implements exact LRU, tracking a full ordered list of every key by access time.
options: True
False
hld-building-blocks:4.explanation: False. Redis uses approximated LRU/LFU: it samples a few keys (maxmemory-samples, default 5) and evicts the best candidate among them. This saves the memory a full linked list over all keys would need.

hld-building-blocks:5.prompt: Which Redis persistence option gives the smallest window of data loss on a crash with reasonable performance?
options: RDB snapshots every 5 minutes
AOF with appendfsync everysec
No persistence with replicas only
AOF with appendfsync no
hld-building-blocks:5.explanation: AOF with fsync every second loses at most about one second of writes and is the common default for durability. RDB every 5 minutes can lose up to 5 minutes, and appendfsync no leaves flushing to the OS, often about 30 s.

hld-building-blocks:5.prompt: How does Redis Cluster decide which node stores a key?
options: Consistent hashing on the full key using virtual nodes
Round-robin across masters as keys are written
CRC16(key) mod 16384 gives a hash slot; each master owns a range of slots
The client chooses any node and Redis replicates to all of them
hld-building-blocks:5.explanation: Redis Cluster has 16,384 hash slots. A key's slot is CRC16(key) mod 16384 (or the hash tag in {}), and slots are assigned to masters. It's not a consistent-hash ring with virtual nodes, though moving slots gives similar rebalancing.

hld-building-blocks:5.prompt: In Redis Cluster, MGET user:1:name user:2:name fails with a CROSSSLOT error. How do you make related keys land in the same slot?
options: Use hash tags, e.g. {user:1}:name and {user:1}:email
Use a longer key prefix like user:
Set cluster-require-full-coverage no
Run the command against a replica instead of the master
hld-building-blocks:5.explanation: Only the substring inside {} is hashed, so keys sharing a hash tag map to the same slot and allow multi-key commands. A shared prefix outside braces doesn't affect hashing, and the coverage setting is about availability, not slots.

hld-building-blocks:5.prompt: What problem does Redis Sentinel solve?
options: Sharding data across multiple masters
Persisting data to disk
Load balancing reads evenly across replicas automatically
Monitoring a master and promoting a replica on failure, then telling clients the new master
hld-building-blocks:5.explanation: Sentinel provides monitoring, automatic failover and service discovery for a single master/replica set. It doesn't shard; that's Redis Cluster. Persistence is RDB/AOF.

hld-building-blocks:5.prompt: A Redis master acknowledges a write, then crashes before replicating it. Sentinel promotes a replica. What happens to that write?
options: It's recovered from the new master's AOF
It's lost, because replication is asynchronous
Sentinel replays it from its own log
The client gets an error retroactively
hld-building-blocks:5.explanation: Redis replication is asynchronous by default, so acknowledged writes not yet on the replica are lost on failover. WAIT can reduce the risk but doesn't make Redis strongly consistent. Sentinel doesn't store data.

hld-building-blocks:5.prompt: Redis is running BGSAVE on a 20 GB dataset with a heavy write load, and memory usage nearly doubles. Why?
options: BGSAVE loads a second copy of the dataset from disk
AOF rewrite and RDB both store data in memory twice
fork() uses copy-on-write; pages modified during the snapshot get duplicated
Replicas send their data back to the master during BGSAVE
hld-building-blocks:5.explanation: BGSAVE forks a child that shares memory pages with the parent. Each page the parent writes during the snapshot is copied, so heavy writes can approach 2x memory. Leave headroom and keep Transparent Huge Pages disabled.

hld-building-blocks:5.prompt: During a network partition, a Redis master is cut off from the majority, which promotes a new master. Clients on the minority side keep writing to the old master. Which setting limits how long those writes are accepted?
options: min-replicas-to-write with min-replicas-max-lag
appendfsync always
maxmemory-policy noeviction
cluster-node-timeout set to 0
hld-building-blocks:5.explanation: min-replicas-to-write makes the master refuse writes when it can't reach enough replicas within the allowed lag, so an isolated old master stops accepting writes that would later be thrown away. fsync settings protect against crashes, not split brain.

hld-building-blocks:5.prompt: Which statements about RDB vs AOF in Redis 7 are correct? Select all that apply.
options: RDB files are compact and fast to load on restart
AOF records write operations and can be rewritten to compact it
RDB guarantees no data loss between snapshots
You can enable both, and Redis uses AOF on restart when it's enabled
AOF with fsync always can never slow down writes
hld-building-blocks:5.explanation: RDB is a compact point-in-time snapshot that loads fast; AOF logs writes and is compacted by rewrite. With both on, Redis loads the AOF because it's more complete. RDB loses everything since the last snapshot, and fsync always is the slowest mode.

hld-building-blocks:5.prompt: Your team uses Redis as a distributed lock for payment processing. Which concerns are valid? Select all that apply.
options: Async replication means a lock can be lost on failover, so two holders are possible
A GC pause can let the lock expire while the holder still thinks it holds it
Use fencing tokens checked by the downstream resource for correctness
SET key value NX PX is atomic, so it's safe from all failure modes
Redis locks never need an expiry because clients always release them
hld-building-blocks:5.explanation: Failover can drop a lock and process pauses can outlive the TTL, so correctness-critical locks need fencing tokens. SET NX PX is atomic on one node but doesn't survive these failures, and a lock without expiry is held forever if the client crashes.

hld-building-blocks:5.prompt: Redis executes commands on a single main thread, so one slow command like KEYS * on a large dataset blocks all other clients.
options: True
False
hld-building-blocks:5.explanation: True. Redis 6+ can use I/O threads for network reads and writes, but commands still run one at a time on the main thread. Use SCAN instead of KEYS, and avoid huge O(N) commands in production.

hld-building-blocks:5.prompt: Redis Cluster supports multi-key transactions across keys stored on different masters.
options: True
False
hld-building-blocks:5.explanation: False. Multi-key commands, MULTI/EXEC and Lua scripts in Redis Cluster must touch keys in the same hash slot. Use hash tags to co-locate keys that need to be updated together.
